headline: Colombia Locks 186,500 Square Miles of Amazon Against Future Mining
meta_description: Days before leaving office, Colombian President Gustavo Petro protected vast Amazon territories from extraction, closing the door on new mining and oil project…
summary_short: Colombia's outgoing president used a 50-year-old law to shield 186,500 square miles of Amazon rainforest from new mining, oil, and gas extraction before his successor ta…
body:
On August 4, 2026, Colombian President Gustavo Petro signed a resolution that will reshape the country's environmental future. The measure placed 186,500 square miles of the Colombian Amazon permanently off-limits to new mining concessions, oil contracts, and gas exploration—a protection that covers an area larger than California. The timing was deliberate: Petro signed just three days before leaving office, knowing his successor had campaigned on reviving oil exploration and legalizing fracking. Existing operations can continue until their contracts expire, but renewal is now impossible. This permanent closure of the door to new extraction represents a rare victory for long-term environmental protection over short-term political cycles.

What made this move remarkable was its legal foundation. Rather than creating a new conservation category, the government invoked Article 47 of the Natural Resources Code, a statute unused at this scale since its creation more than 50 years ago. The resolution rests on deeper legal ground: Colombia's Supreme Court recognized the Amazon as a subject of rights in 2018, and the Constitutional Court reinforced this in 2025 by designating it a specially protected ecosystem. Indigenous territories comprise 55 percent of the protected area—66.2 million acres—and hold 99.5 percent of their forest cover intact while storing approximately 78 percent of the region's carbon.

The stakes extend far beyond Colombia's borders. The Amazon's 400 billion trees release roughly 20 billion tons of water vapor daily into what researchers call flying rivers, which supply moisture for rainfall across Latin America. Around 670 million people depend on these invisible rivers for water. The region stores an estimated 6.5 gigatons of carbon and teeters near a tipping point from which it might transform irreversibly from rainforest into savanna. Yet the resolution's future remains uncertain: the incoming administration, which took office August 7, has not commented on the measure, and because it is an administrative resolution rather than law, it remains vulnerable to reversal.
quick_facts: 186,500 square miles of Colombian Amazon protected from new extraction
Signed August 4, 2026, three days before president left office
Indigenous territories hold 99.5% of their forest cover intact
Amazon releases 20 billion tons of water vapor daily
670 million Latin Americans depend on Amazon's rainfall patterns
